doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Recording technology and engineers over the years
summary: He saw disks, wire and tape; Tippin' In used two mics, and early engineers knew sound better than the electronics.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah. Pass the mege. That was the megaphone. And then all of a sudden, one night, they put up this megaphone and then we played. And in my career, I could say starting with early one morning at Decca Records in 1953 when all this stuff, I saw it all happen. I saw the first wire recorder, I saw the first time on tape, the first time anything — well naturally, I’m 83 years old. And every time we went, now you’ve got to remember that we were with RCA Victor for many years. Erskine’s band was with RCA Victor for ten. We saw the disks, well you know taking it off on disks, and what I really can’t understand, some of the songs like the Tommy Dorsey Band, Artie Shaw, Duke Ellington and even Benny Carter, we did on disk and some of those qualities of these records are the same quality with all this stuff — you know what I mean — with all the electronics and all that. And we never had all that stuff. Like we had, I’ll tell you what, “Tippin’ In” had two mics. Out front for the trumpet and for the piano. That’s it. And if you play that record nowadays, you will notice, look at all of that great stuff that Duke Ellington did over to RCA Victor. that wasn’t any big microphones and each trumpet — I remember one morning we went in to Decca and Sonny Payne, they had such problems recording him until they even turned the drums backwards to get a tune, I can’t think of the name of the tune. The next thing we went in, the engineer said, “Give us all you got. Everything you got.” And this was after we went with King Records. And every time we went in there was always something new about electronics and stuff like that.
Well the bands knew how to balance themselves, didn’t they? You know, from playing live all that time.

Yeah, I guess so. I think that maybe some of the A&R men or people, some of the engineers, I think that maybe they knew more about sound than the electronic sound, because the electronic does it all for himself. You understand what I mean? Because some of the guys we’ve had, I can’t think of the electronic men, the only one I can think of that gave us a couple of hits was a trumpet player named Russ Case. He had left one of the places to come and record with him. But nowadays, look at all this stuff. They’ve four or five, I don’t even know the name of these things. Look at this. You understand? Microphones—
